questions.stem: The Egyptian year was divided into three seasons tied to the Nile. In the correct order, beginning with the flood, they were:
options: akhet (inundation), shemu (growing), peret (harvest)
akhet (inundation), peret (growing), shemu (harvest)
peret (inundation), shemu (growing), akhet (harvest)
shemu (inundation), akhet (growing), peret (harvest)
questions.explanation: Akhet was the season of the flood, peret the season when crops grew as the water went down, and shemu the harvest and low-water season. The order mattered because tax and labour were planned around it.

questions.stem: Officials measured the height of the Nile flood each year with nilometers. The main reason this mattered to the state was that the flood height:
options: set the date on which the king's Heb-Sed jubilee had to be held
showed how many soldiers could be spared for campaigns in Nubia
showed how good the harvest, and so the tax, was likely to be
decided which god would receive the year's booty and foreign tribute
questions.explanation: A good flood watered and enriched more land, so the harvest, and the grain tax assessed on it, could be predicted. A low flood meant hunger, and too high a flood destroyed dykes and villages.

questions.stem: Nubia, south of the First Cataract, was ruled for much of the New Kingdom by an official called the King's Son of Kush. Egypt valued Nubia above all for its:
options: cedar forests, which supplied timber for temple flagstaffs
silver and tin, which Egypt lacked for making bronze tools
olive groves, which supplied oil for temples and the palace
gold, as well as ivory, ebony and recruits for the army
questions.explanation: Nubian gold underpinned Egypt's wealth and its gifts to foreign rulers. Cedar came from Lebanon, and silver had to be imported from western Asia, not Nubia.

questions.stem: Far more New Kingdom evidence survives from Thebes than from the Delta. The main reason is that:
options: Theban scribes wrote on stone, while Delta scribes wrote only on clay tablets
the dry desert edge of Upper Egypt preserves papyri and wood far better
the Delta was almost uninhabited in the New Kingdom, apart from a few forts
the Delta cities were deliberately destroyed by the Hittites after Kadesh
questions.explanation: Thebes' tombs and temples lie on dry desert ground, while the wet, silt-covered Delta has destroyed most organic material. The Delta held major cities, such as the Ramesside capital Pi-Ramesses, so the imbalance is one of survival, not settlement.

questions.stem: A historian writing about ordinary farmers relies mostly on scenes from the tombs of officials and on scribal school texts. The most important problem with this evidence is that it:
options: was made for a literate elite, so farmers appear as the elite saw them
was written in a script that scholars have still not been able to decipher
dates entirely from after the New Kingdom, when farming methods had changed
was produced for foreign visitors and so exaggerates the wealth of Egypt
questions.explanation: Most Egyptians could not read or commission monuments, so their lives are seen through elite eyes, idealised in tombs or belittled in texts praising scribes. Hieroglyphic and hieratic writing have been readable since the nineteenth century.

questions.stem: The Amarna letters are clay tablets in Akkadian cuneiform found at Akhenaten's capital. For the reign of Amenhotep III they are especially useful because they:
options: describe the daily routine of the workmen building the royal tomb
record his gift exchange and marriages with the rulers of Mitanni and Babylon
list every temple estate in Egypt with its fields, workers and annual harvest
give the official Egyptian king list from the founding of the New Kingdom
questions.explanation: Many letters were written to Amenhotep III by rulers of Babylon, Mitanni and smaller states, discussing gold, gifts and royal marriages. They show Egypt as one of a club of great powers.

questions.stem: Ma'at, which every king claimed to uphold, is best defined as:
options: the sacred barque in which Amun travelled at festivals
the name given to the king's living spirit or double
truth, justice and the right order of the universe
the annual tax paid in grain to the royal granaries
questions.explanation: Ma'at was both a concept and a goddess, shown with a feather. The king's duty was to maintain it against isfet, or chaos. The king's spirit was his ka.

questions.stem: Colossal statues, temple reliefs of the king smiting enemies and texts calling him the son of Amun-Ra all served mainly to:
options: persuade foreign kings to send their sons to be educated in Egypt
present the king as the gods' chosen guardian of order
show the king as an ordinary man who owed his throne to the priests
record accurately the number of enemies killed in each campaign
questions.explanation: Royal images followed set conventions that stressed the king's divine role and victory over chaos, whatever the real outcome. Historians therefore read them as ideology rather than as reports of fact.

questions.stem: In the New Kingdom, the vizier's duties included:
options: leading the daily rites before the cult statue of Amun at Karnak
commanding the chariot corps on campaigns in Syria and Palestine
governing Nubia as the king's deputy from a residence at Kerma
judging cases, overseeing officials and reporting to the king
questions.explanation: Texts in the tomb of Rekhmire describe the vizier as chief judge and head of the administration, meeting the king each morning. Rites were the priests' work, and Nubia had its own viceroy.

questions.stem: Horemheb was a general and royal deputy who became king at the end of the 18th Dynasty, and Ramesses I, founder of the 19th Dynasty, was also a military officer. What do these careers suggest?
options: The army had become a route to the highest power in the state
Priests of Amun chose each new king from among the army officers
Only men of royal blood could hold high rank in the army
The army was controlled by the vizier rather than by the king
questions.explanation: Both men rose through military office, and in the absence of a royal heir the army's leaders were well placed to take the throne. Neither was of royal birth, which rules out the claim that high command required royal blood.

questions.stem: Queen Tiye, Great Royal Wife of Amenhotep III, was unusual because she:
options: ruled Egypt as king in her own name for several years after his death
was a Mitannian princess who brought a large dowry of horses and chariots
led an army against the Nubians while the king was ill in Thebes
was of non-royal birth yet was honoured beside the king on scarabs
questions.explanation: Tiye was the daughter of Yuya and Tjuyu, not of a king, yet her name appears with Amenhotep III's on commemorative scarabs and she is shown at equal scale in some statues. Foreign princesses married the king but did not become chief queen.

questions.stem: Ramesses II built a smaller temple beside his own at Abu Simbel, dedicated to Hathor and his Great Royal Wife. This queen was:
options: Nefertari
Nefertiti
Tiye
Ahmose-Nefertari
questions.explanation: The small temple at Abu Simbel honours Nefertari, whose richly painted tomb is in the Valley of the Queens. Nefertiti was Akhenaten's queen and Tiye was Amenhotep III's.

questions.stem: Which statement about non-royal women in the New Kingdom is best supported by the evidence?
options: They could own, buy and sell property and bring cases to court
They could not inherit property, which passed only to sons
They were barred from every kind of temple office and ritual
They regularly served as scribes and officials in the treasury
questions.explanation: Legal documents show women owning land, making wills and going to court, and many served as chantresses in temples. Few women were literate officials, since the bureaucracy was a male career.

questions.stem: Some historians describe Egyptian women as enjoying near-equality with men; others stress that their main roles were as wife and 'mistress of the house'. Which statement best evaluates the debate?
options: Women were equal in every respect, since queens commonly ruled as kings
Women had no rights at all, as tomb scenes never show them
The debate cannot be studied, since no legal documents survive
Women had real legal rights, yet public office and literacy were mostly male
questions.explanation: The legal evidence supports women's property and court rights, but office, literacy and official titles were overwhelmingly held by men. Female kings were very rare, and women appear often in tomb scenes.

questions.stem: Ordinary farmers in the New Kingdom could be called up by the state for:
options: corvee labour on canals, dykes and building works
compulsory training as scribes in the House of Life at Thebes
annual service as priests in the temples of their local gods
duty as jurors in the court of the vizier at the capital
questions.explanation: Peasants owed labour to the state, often during the flood when fields were under water, as well as taxes in grain. The House of Life was a temple scriptorium for educated scribes and priests.

questions.stem: The skilled craftsmen who carved and painted the royal tombs called themselves 'servants in the Place of Truth'. This title tells us that they:
options: were judges who heard disputes in the court of the vizier
were foreign captives settled in Egypt after Thutmose III's wars
worked for the state on the king's tomb, a sacred and restricted task
were temple slaves owned outright by the priests of Amun at Karnak
questions.explanation: The Place of Truth was the royal necropolis, and the Deir el-Medina workmen were state employees paid in rations. Their skills and literacy gave them a higher status than most labourers.

questions.stem: Which military development was central to the New Kingdom army, after the Hyksos period?
options: The war elephant brought from Nubia for frontal charges
The trireme with three banks of oars for war on the Nile
The horse-drawn chariot carrying a driver and an archer
The heavy cavalry horseman wearing iron scale armour
questions.explanation: Chariots and the composite bow, adopted from western Asia during the Hyksos period, became the elite arm of the New Kingdom army. Mounted cavalry and triremes belong to later periods.

questions.stem: The tomb biography of Ahmose son of Ebana at el-Kab records that he received the 'gold of valour', captives and land for his service. This shows that:
options: the army was made up almost entirely of foreign mercenaries from Libya
soldiers were rewarded with wealth and land, so the army brought status
soldiers were unpaid conscripts who returned to farming after each campaign
only the sons of viziers could hold commands in the early New Kingdom
questions.explanation: Ahmose describes fighting under several early 18th Dynasty kings and lists the honours and grants he received. Such rewards made military careers attractive and built a loyal professional army.

questions.stem: New Kingdom Egypt had no coinage. How were officials and workers usually paid?
options: In silver coins stamped with the king's name, issued by the treasury each month
In gold rings weighed out by the priests of Amun at the start of each season
In land grants alone, since the state kept no stores of food or goods
In rations of grain, beer and goods, valued in units such as the deben
questions.explanation: Wages were paid in kind, especially grain, and goods were valued in deben of copper or other units for exchange. Coinage reached Egypt only much later.

questions.stem: Large temples such as Karnak owned fields, herds, ships and workshops, and stored grain in their granaries. In the economy they acted as:
options: markets where farmers sold produce to foreign merchants for silver
military bases that housed the standing army between campaigns
royal palaces where the king lived for most of the year
major landowners and centres that collected and redistributed goods
questions.explanation: Temple estates were a central part of the economy, supporting priests, workers and dependants from their produce. This is one reason the wealth of the Amun temple carried political weight.

questions.stem: Which irrigation device, shown in New Kingdom tomb paintings, uses a weighted pole and bucket to lift water from the river or a canal?
options: the qanat
the noria
the shaduf
the nilometer
questions.explanation: The shaduf let a gardener lift water by hand into channels and gardens. The nilometer measured the flood, while the qanat (an underground channel) and the noria (a water wheel) are not New Kingdom Egyptian devices.

questions.stem: Temple building in Thebes during the New Kingdom made heavy use of sandstone from quarries at Gebel el-Silsila, and granite from Aswan for obelisks. What does this show about the building industry?
options: The state quarried stone and moved it long distances by river
Temples were built of mudbrick only, with stone kept for royal tombs
Stone was imported by sea from Lebanon, since Egypt had no quarries
Each village built its own temple from whatever local stone it found
questions.explanation: Quarry expeditions and Nile barges moved huge blocks downstream to Thebes. The unfinished obelisk at Aswan still shows how granite was worked in the quarry.

questions.stem: The divine family worshipped at Thebes, known as the Theban triad, was:
options: Amun, his consort Mut and their son Khonsu
Osiris, his sister-wife Isis and their son Horus
Ptah, his consort Sekhmet and their son Nefertem
Ra, his daughter Hathor and her son Ihy
questions.explanation: Amun, Mut and Khonsu had temples in the Karnak complex. Osiris, Isis and Horus formed the family central to kingship and the afterlife, and Ptah's triad belonged to Memphis.

questions.stem: During the Opet Festival, the barques of the Theban triad travelled from Karnak to Luxor temple. The festival's main purpose was to:
options: mark the end of the king's thirtieth year with a ritual run
renew the king's divine kingship through his union with Amun
celebrate the harvest by giving the first sheaves to Osiris
mourn the dead and feast with them in the tombs of the west bank
questions.explanation: Opet linked the king with Amun at Luxor, where his royal ka was renewed, and let the people see the god's barque. Feasting with the dead belonged to the Beautiful Feast of the Valley, and the ritual run to the Heb-Sed.

questions.stem: At the Beautiful Feast of the Valley, Amun's barque crossed to the west bank of Thebes. Families at the same time:
options: re-enacted the coronation of the king in the temple of Luxor
visited the tombs of their ancestors to feast and make offerings
were barred from the necropolis while priests purified the tombs
presented the year's tribute from Nubia to the vizier at Karnak
questions.explanation: The festival joined Amun's visit to the royal mortuary temples with family gatherings at the tombs, which reinforced the bond between the living and the dead.

questions.stem: The Heb-Sed festival was:
options: a festival of the dead held in each village cemetery after the harvest
a jubilee renewing the king's strength, first held after about 30 years
the yearly festival of the Nile flood, held when the first water reached Thebes
the coronation ceremony in which a new king first received his royal names
questions.explanation: The Sed festival renewed the king's powers, and included rituals such as a run around a marked course. Amenhotep III and Ramesses II both celebrated several, following the first after about 30 years.

questions.stem: At Deir el-Medina, workmen set up small stelae asking gods such as Ptah or Meretseger for forgiveness and healing, sometimes carved with ears. These stelae are evidence of:
options: the worship of Aten alone, which had replaced the other gods
foreign cults brought to Egypt by Hittite prisoners of war
personal piety, in which individuals sought a direct bond with a god
official temple ritual, which only the king and priests could perform
questions.explanation: Ramesside stelae show people confessing faults and thanking a god for mercy, outside formal temple ritual. The ears represent a god who hears prayers.

questions.stem: Household images of Bes and Taweret were especially associated with:
options: watching over the Nile flood and the grain harvest
protecting mothers and children in childbirth and the home
guarding the king on campaign against foreign enemies
weighing the heart of the dead in the hall of judgement
questions.explanation: Bes, a dwarf-like god, and Taweret, a hippopotamus goddess, protected households, mothers and babies. They appear on amulets, beds and headrests, showing magic in everyday religion.

questions.stem: During mummification, which organ was usually left in the body because Egyptians believed it was needed in the afterlife?
options: the liver
the brain
the stomach
the heart
questions.explanation: The heart, seat of thought and memory, was left in place for the judgement. The liver, lungs, stomach and intestines went into canopic jars, and the brain was removed and discarded.

questions.stem: In the Opening of the Mouth ceremony, a priest touched the mummy or statue with tools such as an adze. The purpose was to:
options: remove the internal organs before the body was dried in natron
record the dead person's name in the temple archives
restore the dead person's ability to eat, breathe and speak
seal the tomb permanently so that robbers could not enter
questions.explanation: The rite magically reanimated the dead so they could receive offerings. Evisceration and drying took place earlier, during embalming.

questions.stem: Spell 125 of the Book of the Dead contains the 'negative confession'. In it the dead person:
options: lists the offerings their family must bring to the tomb each year
names the workmen who built and decorated the tomb
declares before the gods a list of wrongs they did not commit
admits all their sins and begs Osiris to forgive each one
questions.explanation: The dead denied a long list of offences, such as stealing and lying, as part of the judgement before Osiris. The heart was then weighed against the feather of Ma'at.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Book of the Dead from the Amduat?
options: The Book of the Dead was a spell collection for many, while the Amduat traced the sun's night journey in royal tombs
The Book of the Dead was used only by kings, while the Amduat was written on papyri for ordinary people
The Book of the Dead describes the king's coronation, while the Amduat describes the Opet festival
The Book of the Dead dates from the Old Kingdom, while the Amduat was written under the Ptolemies
questions.explanation: Copies of the Book of the Dead were made for elite non-royal burials, while the Amduat, showing the sun god's twelve-hour passage through the underworld, decorated New Kingdom royal tombs. The Book of Gates, used in Ramesside royal tombs, also divides the night into twelve hours.

questions.stem: Luxor temple, built largely under Amenhotep III and enlarged by Ramesses II, was closely linked to:
options: the burial and cult of the Apis bulls of Memphis
the mortuary cult of the female king Hatshepsut
the worship of the Aten as the one and only god
the Opet festival and the king's royal ka
questions.explanation: Luxor temple received Amun's barque from Karnak during Opet and celebrated the king's divine ka. The Apis bulls were buried at Saqqara, and the Aten was Akhenaten's god.

questions.stem: Ramesses III's mortuary temple at Medinet Habu has a gateway built to resemble a fortified tower. Like the Ramesseum of Ramesses II, the temple was mainly intended to:
options: store the weapons of the army for campaigns against the Libyans
serve as the tomb in which the king's mummy was placed
maintain the king's cult and honour Amun after the king's death
house the royal family while the palace at Pi-Ramesses was rebuilt
questions.explanation: Mortuary temples on the west bank provided offerings for the dead king and honoured Amun, while the body lay in a hidden tomb in the Valley of the Kings. Medinet Habu later served as a refuge in troubled times.

questions.stem: Eighteenth Dynasty tombs of Theban officials often show banquets, farming and crafts; many Ramesside private tombs instead show mainly gods, funerary rites and scenes from funerary texts. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Farming and crafts stopped in the Ramesside period, so they were no longer painted
Ramesside officials were forbidden by law to be buried in decorated tombs
The Ramesside tombs were painted by foreign artists unfamiliar with Egyptian life
Tomb decoration shifted towards religious themes, so daily-life scenes are rarer as evidence
questions.explanation: The change reflects religious emphasis, including personal piety, rather than any change in daily activity. For the historian it means Ramesside daily life must be studied more through texts such as the Deir el-Medina ostraca.

questions.stem: The Papyrus Ebers, from the early 18th Dynasty, is valuable to historians because it:
options: collects hundreds of medical remedies and spells
records the trials of tomb robbers in the reign of Ramesses IX
tells the story of a priest's journey to buy cedar in Byblos
lists the gifts sent by Amenhotep III to the king of Babylon
questions.explanation: The Ebers papyrus is one of the largest Egyptian medical texts, mixing practical treatments with magic. It shows that medicine and religion were closely joined.

questions.stem: Wisdom literature such as the Instruction of Any and the Instruction of Amenemope mainly offers:
options: hymns praising the king's victories over foreign enemies in Syria
detailed accounts of tax collected from each province of Egypt
spells to protect the dead on their journey through the underworld
advice on right conduct, such as honesty and self-control
questions.explanation: These instructions pass on moral advice from a father to his son. Amenemope, from the Ramesside period, is well known for passages that parallel the biblical Book of Proverbs.

questions.stem: In the Report of Wenamun, an envoy of Amun's temple sent to Byblos for cedar is robbed on the way and treated with little respect by the local prince. Historians often use it to argue that, by the end of the New Kingdom:
options: Egypt had conquered Byblos and ruled it through a governor
trade with the Levant had ended and Egypt used only local timber
the king had banned temples from sending agents abroad
Egyptian prestige and power in the Levant had greatly declined
questions.explanation: Earlier rulers of Byblos sent timber to Egypt readily, but Wenamun has to bargain and wait. Because it may be partly literary, historians treat it with care, but it fits other evidence of a weaker Egypt.

questions.stem: The Tale of Two Brothers, a Ramesside story, tells how the younger brother Bata is falsely accused by his elder brother's wife and must flee. As a source it is most useful for:
options: an exact record of a court case heard by the vizier at Thebes
the military organisation of the army at the Battle of Kadesh
the measurement of fields for tax by the scribes of the treasury
Ramesside values and ideas about family and the gods
questions.explanation: The tale mixes everyday farm life with magic and divine intervention, so it reveals beliefs and values rather than recording real events. It survives in a papyrus of the 19th Dynasty.
